extracted.intended_audience: AI developers, safety researchers, red teamers, deployers, and policymakers evaluating or deploying large language models (e.g., GPT-4)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for assessing risks, harms, mitigations, and deployment practices for GPT-4–class language models, including red-teaming, system-level interactions, and socio-technical impacts. Focuses on what to test, what to mitigate, and how to prepare for deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate performance across demographic groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate model performance across different demographic groups and tasks; note differences such as decreased performance for speakers of some languages that can lead to disparities in quality of service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure group-differential performance across tasks and languages; consider both representation and allocative harms; be aware that unequal performance can produce disparate quality-of-service outcomes and require careful evaluation before using the model in decision contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict use in high-risk government decisionmaking and prohibitions on legal/health advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage policies prohibit using models and products in contexts of high-risk government decisionmaking (e.g., law enforcement, criminal justice, migration and asylum) or for offering legal or health advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as hard policy constraints when assessing possible deployments; ensure contractual/technical controls prevent such uses and explicitly document prohibited high-risk contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess refusals and mitigation side-effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusals (training the model to refuse certain requests) can mitigate some types of bias but can also exacerbate bias or contribute to a false sense of assurance; unequal refusal behavior across demographics/domains can create quality-of-service harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test refusal behaviors for consistency across demographic groups and prompts; evaluate whether refusals disproportionately affect or protect particular groups; consider trade-offs between refusal frequency and differential impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent generation of hateful, demeaning, or discriminatory content
rubrics_metrics.description: Models must avoid producing content that stereotypes, demeans, or targets groups (examples include offensive jokes about disability/religion or white supremacist bios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use model-level refusals, content policies, and red-team prompt corpora to check for such outputs; provide safe alternatives and ensure the model refuses or redirects when appropriate; measure both false positives and false negatives in refusal behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess disinformation and influence-operation risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the model's capability to generate plausibly realistic, targeted, and persuasive content (news articles, tweets, emails) that could be used to mislead or influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red-team for targeted messaging and persuasive appeals; compare model-generated persuasive content against human-written baselines; test for personalized/targeted disinformation scenarios and the model's ability to produce stepwise plans for influence operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess dual-use proliferation risks (conventional and unconventional weapons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the model can provide information useful to proliferators (nuclear, radiological, biological, chemical), including shortening research time, suggesting vulnerable targets, procurement strategies, or engineering components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform stress testing, boundary testing, and red-team exercises across proliferation-relevant prompts; consider the model's ability to repackage publicly available but hard-to-find information in more accessible forms; account for non-information barriers (equipment, export controls) when estimating real-world risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure hallucination propensity and factual accuracy (especially for long/multi-step responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer responses and multi-step instructions are more likely to contain inaccuracies or hallucinations, which can be persuasive but ultimately wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate factual accuracy across response lengths and multi-step tasks; quantify error rates and the types of hallucinations; prioritize reliability testing in domains where incorrectness is high-risk (e.g., technical instructions, health, legal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate privacy risks—prevent identification and sensitive-personal-data synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Models trained on public and other sources may have knowledge about people with significant online presence and can synthesize multi-step personal or geographic inferences, creating privacy risks and potential identification of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply fine-tuning to reject such requests, remove personal information from training data where feasible, create automated evaluations for privacy leakage, monitor attempts to elicit personal information, and enforce restrictions in terms and policies; improve retrieval tying to user-provided context to reduce spurious inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate cybersecurity dual-use potential (vulnerability discovery and social engineering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the model aids vulnerability discovery, exploitation, or social-engineering tasks (e.g., drafting phishing emails); GPT-4 can explain vulnerabilities in small source files and draft social-engineering content given adequate background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract external cybersecurity experts or red-teamers to probe capabilities on code and social-engineering tasks; test model's ability to produce exploitable code/exploits vs. explanatory outputs; mitigate by training refusals for malicious requests and scaling monitoring/detection systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess potential for risky emergent behaviors (agentic/power-seeking capabilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether models can produce behavior characterized by long-term planning, goal pursuit, autonomous replication, resource acquisition, or instrumentally useful strategies that resemble power-seeking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specialized red-team assessments (e.g., ARC-style experiments) across multiple model versions, including attempts to have the model plan or automate replication/acquisition; assess the effects of fine-tuning and tool-augmented setups; do not rely on early checkpoints only—test final deployed versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate interactions with other systems and tool augmentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Model capabilities can be amplified by chaining with other tools (literature search, molecule search, purchase checks, synthesis planners), producing system-level risks that would not be apparent in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adversarially test model+tool chains in realistic end-to-end workflows; analyze possible feedback loops, emergent abilities, and the potential to find purchasable analogs or automate harmful sequences; require margins of safety for system–system and human–system feedback loops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess economic impacts and distributional effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how deployment may cause workforce displacement, change wages, alter industrial organization, and produce unequal access to benefits of the technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct empirical studies (worker performance experiments, surveys of users and firms), monitor downstream deployments, and study distributional consequences by sector and demographic; plan interventions to mitigate unequal harms from automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess acceleration risk from development and deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how deployment timing, communication strategy, and commercialization might accelerate AI capabilities or encourage racing dynamics that reduce safety standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expert forecasters to predict how different deployment choices (delay length, communications strategy, commercialization method) influence acceleration; consider quieter communication strategies, delayed releases, and coordination with other actors to reduce acceleration risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and mitigate overreliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Overreliance occurs when users excessively trust model outputs despite hallucinations or errors; authoritative tone, hedging, or polished outputs can increase this risk and hinder oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear documentation of capabilities/limitations, incorporate hedging language and refusal behavior carefully, avoid implying human status, train developers to present model outputs with guidance for verification, and monitor downstream developer UI choices that might encourage blind trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation approach for deployment (qualitative & quantitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deployment evaluation should combine qualitative evaluations (expert red-teaming) and quantitative evaluations (automated metrics) to inform mitigation choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design evaluation suites informed by domain experts to decide which automated checks and mitigations are most effective; iterate evaluation across checkpoints and the final model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model-level mitigations: dataset interventions and RLHF
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply dataset filtering (e.g., remove inappropriate erotic content) and post-pretraining interventions such as RLHF using demonstration and ranking data from human trainers to shape behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internally trained classifiers and lexicon-based approaches to flag and remove problematic pretraining documents; collect demonstration and ranking data and apply RLHF as part of behavior shaping; document intervention effects and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: System-level mitigations: UI best practices, monitoring, and detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine model-level changes with system-level mitigations like applying UI best practices to support users, monitoring for usage-policy violations, and scaling internal safety systems to detect bad actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement UX safeguards to reduce overreliance and misuse, instrument monitoring/detection/response pipelines, and use signals from deployments to retrain and improve safety systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red-teaming, stress testing, and boundary testing as evaluation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use adversarial testing techniques (red-teaming, stress testing, boundary testing) to probe model weaknesses across domains including disinformation, dual-use, privacy, emergent behaviors, and system interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate red-team exercises with external experts across domains, iterate tests across model versions, and use findings to prioritize mitigations; document scenarios and concrete prompt examples that elicit harmful behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide margins of safety for system-level feedback loops
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate and plan for system-level emergent risks such as algorithmic collusion, polarization from recommender feedback loops, or correlated decision-making by multiple institutions relying on the same model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adversarially test for feedback-loop effects in context, analyze how correlated reliance across organizations could create systemic risk, and design deployment safeguards or governance to preserve margins of safety.
